(a) In General.—
        (1) Establishment of procedures.—The Attorney General (in judicial districts served by United States trustees) and the Judicial Conference of the United States (in judicial districts served by bankruptcy administrators) shall establish procedures to determine the accuracy, veracity, and completeness of petitions, schedules, and other information that the debtor is required to provide under sections 521 and 1322 of title 11, United States Code, and, if applicable, section 111 of such title, in cases filed under chapter 7 or 13 of such title in which the debtor is an individual. Such audits shall be in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards and performed by independent certified public accountants or independent licensed public accountants, provided that the Attorney General and the Judicial Conference, as appropriate, may develop alternative auditing standards not later than 2 years after the date of enactment of this Act. 
        (2) Procedures.—Those procedures required by paragraph (1) shall—
            (A) establish a method of selecting appropriate qualified persons to contract to perform those audits; 
            (B) establish a method of randomly selecting cases to be audited, except that not less than 1 out of every 250 cases in each Federal judicial district shall be selected for audit; 
            (C) require audits of schedules of income and expenses that reflect greater than average variances from the statistical norm of the district in which the schedules were filed if those variances occur by reason of higher income or higher expenses than the statistical norm of the district in which the schedules were filed; and 
            (D) establish procedures for providing, not less frequently than annually, public information  concerning the aggregate results of such audits including the percentage of cases, by district, in which a material misstatement of income or expenditures is reported.   
    (b) Amendments.—Section 586 of title 28, United States Code, is amended—
        (1) in subsection (a), by striking paragraph (6) and inserting the following:“(6) make such reports as the Attorney General directs, including the results of audits performed under section 603(a) of the Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act of 2005;”; and 
        (2) by adding at the end the following:“(f)(1) The United States trustee for each district is authorized to contract with auditors to perform audits in cases designated by the United States trustee, in accordance with the procedures established under section 603(a) of the Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act of 2005.“(2)(A) The report of each audit referred to in paragraph (1) shall be filed with the court and transmitted to the United States trustee. Each report shall clearly and conspicuously specify any material misstatement of income or expenditures or of assets identified by the person performing the audit. In any case in which a material misstatement of income or expenditures or of assets has been reported, the clerk of the district court (or the clerk of the bankruptcy court if one is certified under section 156(b) of this title) shall give notice of the misstatement to the creditors in the case.“(B) If a material misstatement of income or expenditures or of assets is reported, the United States trustee shall—“(i) report the material misstatement, if appropriate, to the United States Attorney pursuant to section 3057 of title 18; and“(ii) if advisable, take appropriate action, including but not limited to commencing an adversary proceeding to revoke the debtor’s discharge pursuant to section 727(d) of title 11.”.  
    (c) Amendments to Section 521 of Title 11, U.S.C.—Section 521(a) of title 11, United States Code, as so designated by section 106, is amended in each of paragraphs (3) and (4) by inserting “or an auditor serving under section 586(f) of title 28” after “serving in the case”. 
    (d) Amendments to Section 727 of Title 11, U.S.C.—Section 727(d) of title 11, United States Code, is amended—
        (1) in paragraph (2), by striking “or” at the end; 
        (2) in paragraph (3), by striking the period at the end and inserting “; or”; and 
        (3) by adding at the end the following:“(4) the debtor has failed to explain satisfactorily—“(A) a material misstatement in an audit referred to in section 586(f) of title 28; or“(B) a failure to make available for inspection all necessary accounts, papers, documents, financial records, files, and all other papers, things, or property belonging to the debtor that are requested for an audit referred to in section 586(f) of title 28.”.  
    (e) Effective Date.—The amendments made by this section shall take effect 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that independent accountants, public information on audit results, and notice to creditors bring outsiders into a federal decision. But the accountants are contractors carrying out audits of individual bankruptcy cases, not parties consulted on a federal policy decision, and the public information and creditor notices are one-way disclosures. The procedures are set by the Attorney General and the Judicial Conference, both inside the federal government, with no required comment period, hearing, advisory body, outside consultation, or right to sue.
fable.s: performed by independent certified public accountants or independent licensed public accountants

qwen_block.w: This section establishes an audit procedure performed by contracted independent accountants. While these accountants are outside the federal government, they are hired contractors performing a technical verification task, not participants in a consultation, advisory board, or public comment process influencing a federal policy decision. The notification to creditors is a post-hoc disclosure, not a pre-decision consultation or opportunity to object.
qwen_block.s: Such audits shall be in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards and performed by independent certified public accountants or independent licensed public accountants
qwen_block.b:
To determine if this section involves participation, we must analyze the actors and the nature of the interactions described.

1.  **Actors Involved**:
    *   **Federal Government**: The Attorney General, the Judicial Conference of the United States, United States Trustees, Bankruptcy Administrators, the Court/Clerk, and the United States Attorney.
    *   **Outside Parties**: "Independent certified public accountants" or "independent licensed public accountants" (contractors), and "creditors" (who receive notice).

2.  **Nature of Interactions**:
    *   **Audits**: The section establishes procedures for auditing bankruptcy petitions. These audits are performed by independent accountants contracted by federal officials (US Trustees). While the accountants are outside the government, they are hired contractors performing a specific technical task (auditing) defined by federal procedures. This is generally considered an administrative enforcement mechanism rather than "participation" in the sense of consultation, advisory input, or public comment on a policy decision. The definition excludes applications for benefits/grants, and while this isn't an application, it is a compliance check. More importantly, the accountants do not "consult" or "coordinate" with the government to *make* a decision; they provide data *for* the government to make a decision.
    *   **Notice to Creditors**: Subsection (b)(2)(A) states that if a material misstatement is found, the clerk shall "give notice of the misstatement to the creditors in the case." This is a notification *after* a finding has been made. It does not give creditors a right to comment, object, or participate in the decision-making process before the decision is finalized. It is a post-hoc notification.
    *   **Reporting**: The section requires reports to the Attorney General and the filing of audit reports with the court. These are internal government/court procedures.

3.  **Comparison to Definition**:
    *   The definition requires consultation/coordination with outsiders *before* making a decision, or granting a right to sue/object.
    *   Here, the "decision" (finding a misstatement) is made by the auditor (contractor) and confirmed by the US Trustee. The creditors are merely notified. They are not consulted.
    *   The accountants are contractors, not an advisory board or public participants in a policy sense. Their role is technical verification.
    *   There is no public comment period, public hearing, or advisory committee with outside members influencing a federal policy decision.

4.  **Tempting but Wrong Reading**:
    *   One might argue that "independent certified public accountants" are outside parties participating in the process. However, hiring a contractor to perform an audit is standard administrative practice and does not constitute "participation" as defined (consultation/coordination/advisory role in decision-making). The definition emphasizes *consultation* or *coordination* with outsiders like states, tribes, public, etc., to influence a decision. An auditor provides facts, not policy input or consultation.
    *   One might argue that notifying creditors is participation. But notification is not consultation. The creditors have no stated role in the decision-making process here, other than potentially being aware of the misstatement.

5.  **Conclusion**: The section describes an internal audit and enforcement mechanism within the bankruptcy system. It does not involve the federal government consulting with outside parties (like the public, states, or experts in an advisory capacity) to make a decision. The "outside" parties (auditors) are contractors performing a defined task, and creditors are merely notified.

opus.w: Outside accountants are contractors carrying out audits, not advisers consulted before a federal policy decision. Notice to creditors and public release of aggregate results are one-way disclosures. The debtor's chance to explain a misstatement is a defense in an individual case, like Example 11. No comment period, hearing, advisory body, or consultation with states or the public is required.
opus.s: Such audits shall be in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards and performed by independent certified public accountants or independent licensed public accountants
opus.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: Several outside parties appear here, including independent CPAs, creditors, the public and the debtor. That can look like participation. But none of them is consulted before the government makes a policy decision.

- **Auditors:** The independent accountants are hired to perform audits. Doing contracted work is not consulting on a federal decision, and hiring them is a contracting matter, which the definition excludes.
- **Creditors and the public:** Creditors get notice of a misstatement, and the public gets annual summary results. Both are one-way disclosures.
- **The debtor:** The debtor's chance to "explain satisfactorily" a misstatement is a defense in an individual enforcement case, like the manufacturer's response in Example 11.
- **Procedures:** "Establish procedures" does not explicitly call for regulations or public comment.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the publication of aggregate audit results to the public, but this is a post-hoc transparency measure, not a pre-decision consultation or coordination process. The audits are conducted by independent contractors hired by the government, which falls under procurement rather than public participation in decision-making. There is no mechanism for the public or outside entities to advise or influence the federal government's decisions regarding bankruptcy procedures or specific cases.
qwen_chat.s: (D) establish procedures for providing, not less frequently than annually, public information concerning the aggregate results of such audits including the percentage of cases, by district, in which a material misstatement of income or expenditures is reported.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the requirement to provide "public information concerning the aggregate results of such audits" constitutes participation because it involves the general public. However, this is merely a transparency/reporting requirement, not a mechanism for the public to consult with or influence a federal decision before it is made. The definition of participation requires consultation or coordination *before* a decision, or an advisory role. Publishing aggregate statistics after the fact does not fit this definition. Furthermore, the audits themselves are performed by independent contractors (CPAs) hired by the government, which is a procurement/service contract, not a participatory process involving outside parties in the decision-making logic itself. The primary actors are federal officials (Attorney General, Judicial Conference, US Trustees) and contractors.
